rows.experiment_summary: This initial experiment established a minimal RNA-only baseline using PCA (2000 components) with a single profile and no image, aggregation, or fusion, yielding a validation accuracy of 0.485 (F1: 0.464). As the first completed trial, this result serves as the performance reference point against which all subsequent design axes—encoder complexity, multiprofile settings, image modality, and fusion strategies—can be comparatively evaluated. It remains uncertain whether any of these additional components can improve upon this floor, and no comparative conclusions about specific design choices can be drawn from a single data point.
rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero prior information about which modality, encoder, profile setting, or aggregation strategy is most important. The most critical uncertainty is whether the RNA signal alone (with the simplest possible encoder) provides a meaningful performance floor. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the minimal baseline—simplest encoder (PCA), simplest profile (single), single modality. It establishes the performance reference point against which every other axis (encoder complexity, multiprofile, image modality, aggregation, fusion) can be measured. 3) Why it is the best first use of budget: As the first experiment, it maximizes information per trial by anchoring the entire search space. Every subsequent comparison (e.g., config_002 tests multiprofile+avgpool vs. this baseline; config_004 tests scvi vs. PCA; config_016 tests adding image) isolates exactly one or two design decisions relative to this reference. Starting with a more complex configuration would confound multiple variables and make it impossible to attribute performance gains to specific choices under the limited budget.

rows.experiment_summary: This multimodal experiment (single profile, PCA n2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, concat fusion) achieved a validation accuracy of 0.527 (F1: 0.510), a ~4.2-point improvement over the RNA-only baseline (0.485, F1: 0.464) from llm_summary_001. Because the only change relative to that baseline was the addition of the image modality with ResNet50 and concat fusion, the result suggests that incorporating image features provides predictive signal beyond RNA alone under this minimal configuration. However, the relative contributions of the image encoder architecture versus the concat fusion strategy remain unisolated, and it is uncertain whether alternative encoders or more sophisticated fusion mechanisms could yield further gains.
rows.selection_reason: With only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA n2000 → acc 0.485), the dominant uncertainty is whether the image modality contributes any predictive signal beyond RNA. config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, PCA n2000, resnet50, concat) is the cleanest single-axis extension of config_001: it keeps the RNA encoder and profile setting identical and adds only the image modality with the simplest possible fusion (concat) and a standard backbone (resnet50). If it outperforms 0.485, we confirm image adds value and should next probe fusion strategy and image encoder; if it does not, we learn that basic multimodal fusion is insufficient and should focus on RNA encoder upgrades or more sophisticated fusion. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the study's central design question (modality contribution) while changing the fewest variables relative to the existing baseline, making it the most information-dense use of the next budget slot.

rows.experiment_summary: This image-only ablation (ResNet50, single profile, no RNA, no fusion) achieved a validation accuracy of 0.208 (F1: 0.172), substantially below the RNA-only baseline (0.485) from llm_summary_001, indicating that under this minimal configuration the image modality alone carries far less predictive signal than RNA. Taken together with the multimodal result (0.527, llm_summary_002), the ablation triangle suggests the ~4.2-point multimodal gain over RNA-only is primarily attributable to the RNA component, with the image contributing a modest incremental signal on top rather than serving as an independently strong predictor. It remains uncertain whether a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L), alternative fusion mechanisms, or multiprofile settings could substantially alter the image modality's contribution, and the very low image-only performance may reflect limitations of ResNet50 specifically rather than a fundamental lack of information in the image features.
rows.selection_reason: We have RNA-only (0.485) and multimodal+ResNet50+concat (0.527), but we lack the image-only baseline. Without it, the 4.2-point multimodal gain cannot be decomposed: we don't know whether the image encoder alone carries most of the signal, whether the gain is truly synergistic, or whether the concat fusion mechanism is doing the heavy lifting. config_010 (image-only, single profile, ResNet50) is a clean single-axis ablation of config_016 (removing RNA) and a natural complement to config_001. This completes the three-way ablation triangle (RNA-only / image-only / multimodal), which is the most fundamental uncertainty in the current evidence. Resolving it directly informs whether to invest remaining budget in better image encoders (ViT-L), alternative fusion (weighted), or multiprofile settings—making it the highest-information use of the next experiment.

rows.experiment_summary: This RNA-only experiment (single profile, scvi_n200) constitutes a clean single-variable swap relative to the PCA n2000 baseline (llm_summary_001), isolating the effect of a learned nonlinear latent representation versus linear dimensionality reduction. The scvi n200 configuration achieved a validation accuracy of 0.520 (F1: 0.498), a ~3.5-point improvement over PCA n2000 (0.485, F1: 0.464), suggesting that the learned scvi representation captures more predictive structure than PCA even at a substantially lower dimensionality (200 vs. 2000). It remains uncertain whether this encoder advantage persists in multimodal or multiprofile configurations, whether alternative learned encoders (e.g., scGPT) or different latent dimensions could yield further gains, and whether the observed improvement is stable across different random initializations.
rows.selection_reason: Evidence: Three completed experiments establish that RNA (PCA n2000) is the dominant signal source (0.485 acc) while image alone is weak (0.208 acc), and adding ResNet50 image via concat yields a modest +4.2 pt multimodal gain (0.527). The RNA encoder has only been tested as linear PCA, which is a very simple baseline. Uncertainty: It is entirely unknown whether a learned RNA representation (scvi, scGPT) substantially outperforms PCA for the dominant modality. This is the highest-impact unexplored axis because the RNA encoder choice will propagate to every future multimodal configuration. Question: config_004 (RNA-only, single profile, scvi_n200) changes exactly one variable relative to config_001 (PCA n2000 → scvi n200), cleanly isolating the effect of a learned latent representation versus linear dimensionality reduction. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a minimal, single-variable comparison that reduces uncertainty about the most fundamental design choice (RNA representation quality) before investing budget in more complex multimodal, multiprofile, or fusion variants. If scvi substantially improves over PCA, it justifies exploring scvi-based multimodal configs; if it does not, PCA remains the preferred encoder and we can focus budget on other axes (multiprofile, image encoder, fusion). This is more informative than testing fusion strategy or image encoder, which affect a weaker modality, and more informative than multiprofile configs, which change two variables simultaneously (profile setting + aggregation).

rows.experiment_summary: This multimodal experiment (single profile, scvi_n200, ResNet50, concat) achieved a validation accuracy of 0.536 (F1: 0.516), a ~0.9-point improvement over the otherwise identical PCA n2000 configuration (0.527, F1: 0.510; llm_summary_002), confirming that the scvi encoder advantage seen in the RNA-only setting (~3.5 pts, llm_summary_004) persists in the multimodal context, albeit at a reduced magnitude. This establishes scvi_n200 as the preferred RNA encoder for subsequent multimodal and multiprofile experiments. It remains uncertain whether the attenuated gain reflects partial redundancy between the learned nonlinear latent and image features under concat fusion, whether alternative fusion strategies or multiprofile settings could further widen the encoder gap, and whether the result is stable across random initializations.
rows.selection_reason: Evidence: config_004 showed scvi_n200 outperforms PCA n2000 by ~3.5 points in the RNA-only setting (0.520 vs 0.485), and config_016 established that the best multimodal result so far (0.527) uses PCA n2000 with ResNet50 and concat fusion. Uncertainty: it is unknown whether the scvi representation advantage persists when image features are also present, since the learned nonlinear latent may interact differently with the concat fusion than a linear PCA projection. This experiment (config_028: multimodal, single profile, scvi_n200, ResNet50, concat) is a clean single-variable swap of the RNA encoder relative to config_016, isolating the encoder effect in the multimodal context. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it directly exploits the strongest evidence we have (scvi > PCA) in the regime where we expect the highest absolute performance, and the outcome will determine which RNA encoder to carry forward into all subsequent multiprofile and fusion-strategy experiments, thereby reducing uncertainty on the most impactful design axis before adding further complexity.

rows.experiment_summary: This multimodal multiprofile experiment (scvi_n200, ResNet50, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) achieved a validation accuracy of 0.632 (F1: 0.607), a ~9.5-point improvement over the single-profile counterpart (0.536, F1: 0.516; llm_summary_005) with all other settings held constant. The result suggests that aggregating multiple profiles provides substantial additional predictive signal beyond a single profile under the established best encoder and fusion configuration, making multiprofile the most impactful design axis explored so far. It remains uncertain whether the gain is driven primarily by the multiprofile data itself, the avgpool aggregation method, or their interaction, and whether more sophisticated aggregation strategies (e.g., transformer-based) could yield further improvements on top of this new baseline.
rows.selection_reason: Evidence: Five experiments have established that (a) RNA dominates over image (0.485 vs 0.208 standalone), (b) scvi_n200 outperforms PCA n2000 in both RNA-only (+3.5 pts) and multimodal (+0.9 pts) settings, and (c) the current best is config_028 (scvi_n200 + ResNet50, concat, single profile) at 0.536 acc. However, the multiprofile axis is completely unexplored—no experiment has tested whether aggregating multiple profiles provides additional predictive signal beyond a single profile. Question: Does multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation improve upon the single-profile multimodal baseline, and if so, by how much? This isolates the profile/aggregation effect while holding all other variables (scvi_n200, ResNet50, concat) at their established best settings. Why this experiment: It probes the largest unexplored design axis (profile setting + aggregation) with the minimal necessary change (single→multiprofile, which inherently requires an aggregation method; avgpool is the simplest). If multiprofile+avgpool yields a clear gain, the next experiment can test whether transformer aggregation adds further value. If it does not, we learn that the single profile already captures the relevant signal, saving budget from pursuing more complex aggregation strategies. This is more informative than testing a fusion swap (weighted vs concat, likely small effect) or an image encoder upgrade (ViT-L), given the image modality's very weak standalone performance (0.208) suggests limited complementary information regardless of encoder quality.

rows.experiment_summary: This multimodal multiprofile experiment (scvi_n200, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) achieved a validation accuracy of 0.688 (F1: 0.659), a ~5.6-point improvement over the otherwise identical avgpool configuration (0.632, F1: 0.607; llm_summary_006), indicating that a learned, position-aware transformer aggregation captures inter-profile interaction signal that symmetric averaging discards. Because the only change was the aggregation method, the result isolates aggregation design as a consequential axis beyond the multiprofile data-volume gain and establishes transformer as the preferred default for subsequent experiments. It remains uncertain whether further aggregation architectures could yield additional gains, whether the observed improvement is stable across random initializations, and how this choice interacts with alternative encoders or fusion strategies.
rows.selection_reason: The largest single gain in this study came from switching to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation (+9.5 pts, config_030: 0.632 vs config_028: 0.536), making the aggregation method the most consequential unexplored axis. The only aggregation tested so far is avgpool, which treats all profiles symmetrically. config_032 (scvi_n200, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat) is a clean single-variable swap from config_030, isolating whether a learned, position-aware aggregation (transformer) captures inter-profile interactions that simple averaging discards. If transformer significantly outperforms avgpool, it indicates that profile ordering/interaction carries predictive signal and justifies further investment in aggregation design; if it is comparable, it confirms the multiprofile gain is primarily from increased data volume, simplifying the design space. This is the highest-value next experiment because it directly probes the mechanism behind the study's largest observed effect, and the result will inform whether subsequent experiments (e.g., with ViT-L or scGPT) should use avgpool or transformer as the default aggregation.

rows.experiment_summary: This multimodal multiprofile experiment (scvi_n200, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) achieved a validation accuracy of 0.713 (F1: 0.695), a ~2.5-point improvement over the otherwise identical concat-fusion configuration (0.688, F1: 0.659; llm_summary_007), isolating the effect of learned modality weighting over simple concatenation. The result suggests that weighted fusion captures complementary modality contributions that concat alone does not fully exploit, establishing it as the preferred fusion default under the current best settings. It remains uncertain whether the gain is stable across random initializations, whether more complex fusion mechanisms (e.g., attention-based gating) could yield further improvements, and how this fusion choice interacts with alternative encoder or image-architecture choices.
rows.selection_reason: The current best configuration (config_032: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, ResNet50, transformer, concat; acc 0.688) has only been tested with concat fusion. Fusion strategy is the one major design axis that remains completely unexplored—every completed experiment used either no fusion or concat. Config_033 is a clean single-variable swap (concat → weighted) under the established best settings, directly isolating whether learned modality weighting provides additional gain over simple concatenation. This is the highest-information next step because: (1) it exploits the current best direction with minimal risk, (2) it tests an axis that could interact with all other choices (encoder, aggregation, profile setting), and (3) under a limited budget, ruling in or out the fusion axis before investing in more complex changes (e.g., ViT-L, scGPT) ensures subsequent experiments build on the correct fusion default. If weighted fusion improves on 0.688, it is a direct gain; if not, concat is confirmed as sufficient and we can focus remaining budget on encoder or image-architecture questions.

The current best (config_033: scvi_n200, ResNet50, transformer, weighted, 0.713) has been built by sequentially optimizing RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation, and fusion. The one major axis still unexplored in this best configuration is the image encoder architecture—we have only ever used ResNet50, which produced very weak image-only performance (0.208). Config_039 swaps only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l while holding all other settings (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) constant, giving a clean single-variable comparison. This tests whether the modest ~0.9-pt multimodal gain over RNA-only is an artifact of a weak image encoder or reflects a fundamental ceiling on image signal. A strong positive result would identify a new exploitable axis; a null result would confirm that further image-encoder investment is unlikely to help and redirect budget toward RNA-encoder alternatives (e.g., scgpt) or other structural changes. Under the limited budget, this is the highest-information next step because it resolves uncertainty on an entirely untested axis while remaining a direct exploitation of the current best configuration.
